text: Saba Valadkhan (Persian: صبا ولدخان) is an Iranian American biomedical scientist who serves as an Assistant Professor and RNA researcher at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio.[1] In 2005, she received the GE / Science Young Scientist Award for her groundbreaking work on the mechanism of spliceosomes—described as "akin to finding the Holy Grail of the splicing catalysis field"[2]—a field critical because "20 percent or 30 percent of all human genetic diseases are caused by mistakes that the spliceosome makes."[3] She earned her medical degree from Tehran University of Medical Sciences in Iran in 1996 and moved to the United States to pursue her Ph.D. at Columbia University, New York.[4] In 2004, she joined Case Western Reserve University as an Assistant Professor.[5] Her research focuses on the role of small nuclear RNAs in the human spliceosome under the supervision of Prof. James Manley.[2] She has developed a novel minimal spliceosome consisting of only two spliceosomal snRNAs that catalyzes a reaction identical to the natural splicing reaction. This system provides direct evidence for RNA catalysis in the spliceosome, thereby resolving the long-standing question of the catalytic domain's identity, and also serves as a powerful tool for studying the structure and function of the spliceosome. Valadkhan was awarded the Harold Weintraub award from the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center in Seattle for her doctoral thesis.[4] She was named a Searle Scholar in 2004 and also received the American Association for Advancement of Science (AAAS) Young Scientist Grand Prize that same year.[4][6] In 2006, she became a founding member of the Rosalind Franklin Society and was honored with the Nsoroma Award from the Cleveland Chapter of the National Technical Association.[7]
